AAL Apparel: Q4 2020 Sales Analysis (Australia)¶

Course: Applied Data Science with Python (course-end project)

Business goal: AAL's head of Sales and Marketing needs to know which states generate the most revenue, and which sales programs to run in the weaker states. This report covers data wrangling, analysis, a visual dashboard and a set of recommendations, using AusApparalSales4thQrt2020.csv (October to December 2020, 7 states, 4 demographic groups, 3 times of day).

Finding: there are no missing values, no duplicates and no impossible values, but the Time, State and Group labels all carry a leading space (e.g. ' WA'), which would silently break filters and merges, so they are stripped. The Date column was text (1-Oct-2020) and is now a datetime, covering 90 consecutive days with a complete 7 states x 4 groups x 3 time slots (84 rows) every day. Sales is exactly 2,500 per unit in every row, so Sales and Unit carry the same information up to a constant.

1.2 Recommendations for treating missing and incorrect data¶

Because nothing is missing here, no rows need to be dropped or filled. For future extracts the recommended policy is:

  • Few missing values (under about 5%) in a numeric column such as Unit or Sales: fill rather than drop, using the median of the same State, Group and Time slot (the median is robust to the large sales peaks seen in this data). Where Sales is missing but Unit is known, derive it as Unit x 2,500; where Unit is missing, derive it as Sales / 2,500. This uses the exact relationship found above and introduces no bias.
  • Missing categorical keys (State, Group, Time) or Date: drop the row, or flag it for review, since it cannot be assigned to a segment and guessing would distort the group-wise totals.
  • Incorrect entries (negative values, typos in labels, mixed date formats): standardise labels with str.strip() and a lookup table, and verify against the source system rather than silently deleting.
  • Dropping is only appropriate when a whole day or whole segment is unreliable; dropping scattered rows would create gaps in the daily series used for the weekly and monthly reports.

1.3 Data normalisation (min-max)¶

Normalisation (min-max scaling to the 0-1 range) is chosen over standardisation, as recommended in the brief: Sales and Unit are strictly positive, not normally distributed, and a bounded 0-1 scale is easy to compare across the two columns and to show on a dashboard.

1.4 groupby() for data chunking and merging: insights and recommendation¶

In [5]:
# chunking: split the data into segments and summarise each
by_state = df.groupby('State').agg(Sales=('Sales','sum'), Units=('Unit','sum'), Rows=('Sales','size'))
print(by_state.sort_values('Sales', ascending=False))
# merging: build a summary table from separately grouped pieces and join them
state_tot = df.groupby('State')['Sales'].sum().rename('state_sales')
grp_tot = df.groupby(['State','Group'])['Sales'].sum().rename('group_sales').reset_index()
merged = grp_tot.merge(state_tot, on='State'); merged['share_of_state_%'] = (merged['group_sales'] / merged['state_sales'] * 100).round(1)
print(); merged.head(8)

Insight and recommendation: groupby() is the right tool for chunking: it splits the 7,560 transactions into State, Group, Time or calendar-period segments and aggregates each in one pass. Summaries built from different groupings can then be merged back (as above, to get each group's share of its state). Recommended practice: use groupby with named aggregations to build one tidy summary table per business question (state, group, time-of-day, week, month), and merge those tables into the report rather than looping over the raw rows. It is faster, less error-prone and keeps every number traceable to the raw data.

2.3 Weekly, monthly and quarterly reports¶

In [9]:
df['Week'] = df['Date'].dt.to_period('W-SUN').apply(lambda p: p.start_time.date())   # weeks start Monday
df['Month'] = df['Date'].dt.strftime('%b %Y')
df['Quarter'] = df['Date'].dt.to_period('Q').astype(str)
def report(col, order=None):
    r = df.groupby(col).agg(Sales=('Sales','sum'), Units=('Unit','sum'), Avg_Sales_per_row=('Sales','mean')).round(0)
    if order: r = r.loc[order]
    r['share_%'] = (r.Sales / r.Sales.sum() * 100).round(1); return r
weekly = report('Week'); monthly = report('Month', ['Oct 2020','Nov 2020','Dec 2020']); quarterly = report('Quarter')
print('WEEKLY'); print(weekly); print('\nMONTHLY'); print(monthly); print('\nQUARTERLY'); print(quarterly)
METRICS['best_month'] = monthly.Sales.idxmax(); METRICS['worst_month'] = monthly.Sales.idxmin()
METRICS['best_week'] = str(weekly.Sales.idxmax()); METRICS['worst_week'] = str(weekly.Sales.idxmin())

  • Quarterly: the data covers a single quarter (2020-Q4), so the quarterly report is one row with total sales and units.
  • Monthly: the monthly table shows the best and worst month; December is the strongest month (A$135.3M, 39.8%), October is second (A$114.3M) and November is the weakest (A$90.7M, 26.6%): sales dip in November and then jump from the last days of November onward.
  • Weekly: the first and last weeks are partial (1 Oct is a Thursday and 30 Dec a Wednesday), so judge the week-on-week trend on the full weeks only. The two partial weeks (first and last) are the smallest in the table for that reason.

3.5 Visualisation package recommendation¶

Recommendation: Seaborn (on top of Matplotlib). Seaborn gives statistical plots (box plots, distribution/KDE plots, heatmaps, grouped bars with automatic aggregation) in one line each, has clean defaults suited to a management audience, and works directly on pandas DataFrames, which suits a groupby-centred analysis. Matplotlib is still used underneath for layout and saving figures. Plotly would add interactivity (hover, drill-down) and is a good next step if the dashboard is deployed to a live app, but for a static JupyterLab report Seaborn is simpler, reproducible and prints well.

Key findings¶

  1. Highest-revenue states: Victoria (A$105.6M, 31% of sales), NSW (A$75.0M, 22%) and SA (A$58.9M, 17%). **Lowest:** WA (A$22.2M), NT (A$22.6M) and TAS (A$22.8M); VIC sells about 4.8x WA.
  2. Demographic groups each contribute about a quarter of sales (Men highest at 25.2%, Seniors lowest at 24.7%); no single group explains the state gap.
  3. Time of day: sales are spread very evenly: Morning is the peak (33.6%), Evening the off-peak (32.9%).
  4. Seasonality: December is the strongest month and November the weakest, a network-wide pattern.

Recommendations for AAL¶

  • Lower-revenue states: run targeted sales programs in the bottom three states (WA, NT and TAS): bundle and promotional offers in the strongest-selling group of each state, local marketing, and loyalty offers, then measure uplift against the Q4 baseline in this report.
  • Learn from the top states: replicate their mix of group offers and store hours in comparable cities of the weaker states.
  • Time-of-day offers: use the off-peak slot for hyper-personalised "next best offer" messages and short promotions, and staff and stock to the peak slot.
  • Seasonality: plan inventory and campaigns around the December peak; use the soft November period for promotions and acquisition offers.
  • Expansion: weigh investment toward states with strong sales and clear headroom; a longer history (full year) is needed before committing, since this is a single quarter.

Limitations: one quarter of data only; Sales is exactly Unit x 2,500 in every row so there is no price variation to analyse; the data has no costs or margins, so revenue ranks do not imply profit.
